facts.fact: Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498 and was received by the Zamorin.
The Dutch set up their first factory at Masulipatnam in 1605.
At Plassey (1757) Clive defeated Siraj-ud-Daulah.
Fort Geldria at Pulicat was the headquarters of Dutch Coromandel.
The First Carnatic War ended with the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748).
Sir Eyre Coote defeated Count de Lally at Wandiwash (1760).
Broach was among the earliest English factories (first quarter of the 17th century).
Bengal staple exports were cotton textiles, raw silk, saltpetre and opium.
The Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle restored Madras to the English.
The Nizam confirmed the Northern Circars to the British by treaty in 1766, after Shah Alam II's farman of 1765.
The Charter Act of 1813 ended the EIC monopoly except for tea and the China trade.
Albuquerque captured Goa from Bijapur in 1510.
The Danes set up their factory at Tranquebar (1620).
Yanam was a French enclave that merged with India in 1954.
The Northern Circars were Srikakulam, Rajahmundry, Eluru, Kondapalli and Guntur.
At Buxar (1764) Hector Munro defeated Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daulah and Shah Alam II.
Machilipatnam was the chief Golconda port with Dutch, English and French factories.
St Francis Xavier is entombed at the Basilica of Bom Jesus in Old Goa.
Ziegenbalg began the first Protestant mission at Tranquebar in 1706.
The Treaty of Allahabad (1765) gave the Company the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.
Almeida's Blue Water Policy aimed at mastery of the sea.
The Portuguese won the naval Battle of Diu (1509).
Goa became the Portuguese capital in 1530 under Nino da Cunha.
Goa, Daman and Diu were liberated in 1961.
Clive's capture of Arcot (1751) was the turning point of the Second Carnatic War.
Francois Martin founded Pondicherry in 1674.
The Danes sold their Indian settlements to the British in 1845.
Mir Jafar's betrayal won Plassey for Clive.
The English factory at Surat (1613) followed the Battle of Swally.
The order of arrival was Portuguese, Dutch, English, Danish, French.
Bartholomeu Diaz rounded the southern tip of Africa in 1487 and called it the Cape of Storms.
Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in May 1498 with three ships, guided across the Arabian Sea by a Gujarati pilot (Abdul Majid).
Pedro Alvares Cabral led the second Portuguese voyage to Calicut in 1500.
Vasco da Gama returned in 1502 and bombarded Calicut.
The second Portuguese fort was built at Cannanore in 1505.
Francisco de Almeida (1505–09) was the first Portuguese viceroy in India.
At the Battle of Chaul (1508) the Egyptian–Gujarati fleet defeated the Portuguese and killed Almeida's son.
Under the cartaz system, Indian ships had to buy a Portuguese pass to sail the Arabian Sea.
Albuquerque took Goa in 1510 from Yusuf Adil Shah, the Sultan of Bijapur.
Albuquerque banned sati in Goa and encouraged Portuguese men to marry Indian women.
The Portuguese introduced tobacco, cashew and new coconut varieties into India.
Nino da Cunha obtained Bassein from Bahadur Shah of Gujarat by the Treaty of Bassein (1534).
Bahadur Shah let the Portuguese build a fort at Diu (1535); he drowned in a scuffle with them in 1537.
The Portuguese captured Daman in 1559.
The Portuguese set up the first printing press in India at Goa in 1556.
The Goa Inquisition began in 1560.
The Portuguese settled at Hugli (c.1579) under a grant from Akbar; Shah Jahan captured it in 1632.
San Thome (Mylapore) near Madras and Chittagong in Bengal were Portuguese settlements.
The Portuguese lost all their Malabar forts, including Cochin, to the Dutch by 1663.
The Portuguese acquired Dadra and Nagar Haveli from the Marathas in 1779.
Panjim (Nova Goa) became the capital of Portuguese India in 1843.
Goa, Daman and Diu were liberated by Operation Vijay in December 1961.
Portuguese decline is blamed on religious intolerance (Jesuits), piracy and the rise of the Dutch and English.
The Dutch United East India Company (VOC) was formed in 1602.
The Dutch set up at Pulicat in 1610 and built Fort Geldria there.
The Dutch opened a factory at Surat in 1616.
The Dutch had factories at Palakollu, Draksharama and Bheemunipatnam on the Andhra coast.
The Dutch factory at Chinsura in Bengal (Fort Gustavus) dates from 1653.
The Dutch took Nagapattinam from the Portuguese (1659) and made it their Coromandel HQ in 1690.
The Dutch captured Cochin from the Portuguese in 1663.
The Amboyna Massacre (1623) of English traders by the Dutch made the English leave the spice islands.
At Colachel (1741) Marthanda Varma of Travancore defeated the Dutch and captured Eustachius De Lannoy.
At Bedara (1759) the English under Colonel Forde crushed the Dutch in Bengal.
By the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824 the Dutch handed their Indian settlements to the British.
The Dutch ran a carrying (redistributive) trade — Indian textiles bought to pay for Indonesian spices.
The Danish East India Company was founded in 1616 under King Christian IV.
Ove Gjedde got Tranquebar from Raghunatha Nayak of Thanjavur in 1620 and built Fort Dansborg.
Serampore (Frederiksnagore) near Calcutta was the chief Danish settlement in Bengal (from 1755).
The Danes are better known for missionary work than for trade.
The Danes sold Tranquebar and Serampore to the British in 1845.
The EIC's charter (31 Dec 1600) gave 'The Governor and Company of Merchants of London Trading into the East Indies' a 15-year monopoly.
The first EIC voyage (1601) under James Lancaster went to Sumatra and Java.
Captain William Hawkins came on the ship Hector (1608) to Jahangir, who called him English Khan, but the Portuguese blocked a Surat factory.
The English opened their first east-coast factory at Masulipatnam in 1611 (ship Globe).
Captain Thomas Best beat the Portuguese at Swally (Suvali) near Surat in 1612.
Sir Thomas Roe, ambassador of James I, stayed at Jahangir’s court 1615–1619.
The English built a factory at Armagaon (Durgarajupatnam, Nellore) in 1626.
The Golconda Sultan's 'Golden Farman' (1632) let the English trade freely in Golconda ports for 500 pagodas a year.
The English opened factories at Hariharpur and Balasore in Orissa in 1633.
Francis Day leased Madras (1639) from Damarla Venkatadri Nayaka, an agent of the Vijayanagara (Chandragiri) king.
Shah Shuja allowed the English a factory at Hugli (1651) for Rs 3,000 a year.
Charles II leased Bombay to the Company in 1668 for £10 a year.
Gerald Aungier is regarded as the founder of Bombay; the HQ shifted from Surat to Bombay in 1687.
Child's War (1686–90) — Josiah Child's attack on Aurangzeb — ended in English defeat and a fine.
Job Charnock set up a factory at Sutanati in 1690, the start of Calcutta.
In 1698 the Company bought the zamindari of Sutanati, Kalikata and Gobindapur.
Fort William (Calcutta) was completed in 1700 with Charles Eyre as first President.
The rival English Company (1698) merged with the old one in 1708 as the United Company of Merchants.
Farrukhsiyar's farman of 1717 (Surman embassy) — the Company's 'Magna Carta' — gave duty-free Bengal trade for Rs 3,000 a year.
A dastak was a free pass exempting Company goods from transit duty; its misuse by servants angered the Nawabs.
The English had a factory at Visakhapatnam from 1682.
The French Compagnie des Indes Orientales was founded in 1664 by Colbert under Louis XIV as a state company.
Francois Caron set up the first French factory at Surat in 1668.
The French got a factory at Masulipatnam (1669) from the Sultan of Golconda.
Sher Khan Lodi, Bijapur governor of Valikondapuram, granted Francois Martin the site of Pondicherry (1673).
Chandernagore was granted by Shaista Khan, the Mughal governor of Bengal, in 1690.
The Dutch took Pondicherry in 1693 but gave it back under the Treaty of Ryswick (1697).
The French acquired Mahe (Malabar) in 1725, Yanam in 1731 and Karaikal in 1739.
Lenoir and Dumas were French governors before Dupleix (1742).
Dupleix became Governor of Pondicherry in 1742 (the PDF says 1741).
The French were the first Europeans to recruit Indians as soldiers (sepoys) in a European-style army.
Count de Lally was executed in Paris in 1766 for the loss of French India.
Chandernagore passed to India in 1950 and merged with West Bengal in 1954.
Pondicherry, Karaikal, Mahe and Yanam were transferred de facto on 1 November 1954; the de jure cession came in 1962.
The First Carnatic War was an extension of the War of Austrian Succession in Europe.
La Bourdonnais, governor of Mauritius (Isle de France), captured Madras for the French in September 1746.
At St Thome on the Adyar (1746) a small French force beat the Carnatic Nawab Anwaruddin's army under Mahfuz Khan.
By Aix-la-Chapelle (1748) Madras was returned to the English in exchange for Louisbourg in North America.
At the Battle of Ambur (1749) Anwaruddin was killed by the French–Chanda Sahib–Muzaffar Jung alliance.
In the Second War the French backed Chanda Sahib (Carnatic) and Muzaffar Jung (Hyderabad); the English backed Muhammad Ali and Nasir Jung.
After Muzaffar Jung was murdered (1751), Bussy placed Salabat Jung on the Hyderabad throne.
Clive took Arcot (31 Aug 1751) and held it through a 53-day siege to relieve Trichinopoly.
Chanda Sahib was defeated and executed (1752), leaving Muhammad Ali as Nawab of the Carnatic.
Godeheu replaced Dupleix (1754) and signed the Treaty of Pondicherry (1754–55).
The Treaty of Pondicherry bound both companies not to interfere in the quarrels of Indian princes.
The Third Carnatic War was the Indian theatre of the Seven Years’ War (1756–63).
Clive and Admiral Watson captured French Chandernagore in March 1757.
Lally captured Fort St David (Cuddalore) in 1758 but failed to take Madras (1758–59).
The Battle of Wandiwash was fought on 22 January 1760; Bussy was taken prisoner.
Pondicherry surrendered to Eyre Coote in January 1761 (the PDF says February) and Mahe fell the same year.
The Treaty of Paris (1763) returned Pondicherry and Chandernagore to France but forbade fortification.
English success came from naval superiority, Bengal’s wealth and the backing of the Company’s home government.
Murshid Quli Khan made Bengal virtually independent and moved the capital to Murshidabad.
Alivardi Khan (1740–56), grandfather of Siraj, kept the Europeans unfortified and fought the Maratha raids.
Holwell claimed 146 English were locked in the Black Hole (June 1756) and 123 died.
Siraj renamed Calcutta Alinagar; the Treaty of Alinagar (Feb 1757) restored English privileges.
The Plassey conspiracy included Mir Jafar, Rai Durlabh, Jagat Seth, Omichand and Manikchand.
Mir Madan and Mohan Lal stayed loyal to Siraj at Plassey.
Plassey (Palashi) lies on the Bhagirathi river; Alamgir II was the Mughal emperor then.
Siraj was killed by the men of Miran, Mir Jafar's son.
Mir Jafar gave the Company the zamindari of the 24 Parganas.
Mir Qasim (1760) gave the Company Burdwan, Midnapore and Chittagong.
Mir Qasim moved his capital from Murshidabad to Monghyr (Munger) and abolished internal duties for all.
The Battle of Buxar was fought on 22 October 1764.
Under the Treaty of Allahabad the Company paid Shah Alam II Rs 26 lakh a year and gave him Kara and Allahabad.
Shuja-ud-Daulah paid Rs 50 lakh and Awadh was kept as a buffer state.
Clive's Dual Government (1765–72) gave the Company the diwani while the Nawab kept the nizamat.
Muhammad Reza Khan (Bengal) and Shitab Rai (Bihar) were the deputy diwans.
Warren Hastings ended the Dual Government in 1772.
The great Bengal famine of 1770 killed about a third of the population.
Bussy obtained the Northern Circars from Salabat Jung in 1753 to pay French troops.
Colonel Forde beat Conflans at Condore (Chandurthi, near Peddapuram) in December 1758.
Forde stormed Masulipatnam in April 1759, ending French power in the Circars.
Salabat Jung then ceded Masulipatnam and nearby territory to the English (1759).
Under the 1766 treaty with the Nizam the Company agreed to pay tribute and supply troops for the Circars.
The Guntur Circar was held by the Nizam's brother Basalat Jung until his death (1782); it was handed over in 1788.
The Nizam ceded the Rayalaseema 'Ceded Districts' to the British in 1800 under his subsidiary alliance.
Thomas Munro was the first Principal Collector of the Ceded Districts.
Hyder Ali rose as faujdar of Dindigul (1755) and set up a modern arsenal with French help.
The First Anglo-Mysore War (1767–69) ended with the Treaty of Madras, a mutual-defence pact dictated near Madras.
In the Second War Eyre Coote defeated Hyder Ali at Porto Novo (1781); Hyder died in 1782.
The Second Anglo-Mysore War ended with the Treaty of Mangalore (1784), restoring mutual conquests.
Tipu's attack on Travancore (1789) led Cornwallis to declare the Third War (1790–92).
By the Treaty of Seringapatam (1792) Tipu gave up half his kingdom (Malabar, Coorg, Dindigul, Baramahal) and paid Rs 3 crore.
In the Fourth War (1799) under Wellesley, Tipu died defending Seringapatam (4 May 1799).
After 1799 a Wodeyar boy, Krishnaraja III, was restored to a smaller Mysore under a subsidiary alliance.
Tipu planted a Tree of Liberty at Seringapatam and joined the Jacobin Club.
Raghunathrao signed the Treaty of Surat (1775) with Bombay, giving Salsette and Bassein for help.
Nana Phadnavis led the Barbhai council of twelve that ruled for the infant Sawai Madhavrao.
The Treaty of Purandar (1776) — by the Calcutta council — annulled the Treaty of Surat.
Surrounded at Wadgaon, the English signed the humiliating Convention of Wadgaon (1779).
The Treaty of Salbai (1782), mediated by Mahadji Scindia, ended the First War and kept peace for 20 years.
Peshwa Baji Rao II accepted a subsidiary alliance by the Treaty of Bassein (31 Dec 1802) after losing to Holkar.
Arthur Wellesley defeated Scindia and Bhonsle at Assaye (1803); Lake won at Laswari.
Bhonsle signed the Treaty of Deogaon (1803), ceding Cuttack and Balasore.
Scindia signed the Treaty of Surji-Arjangaon (1803), ceding the Ganga–Yamuna doab, Delhi and Agra.
Holkar signed the Treaty of Rajpurghat (1805).
The Third War (1817–18) under Lord Hastings grew out of the campaign against the Pindaris.
The Peshwa lost at Khadki (Kirkee) and Koregaon; Bhonsle at Sitabuldi; Holkar at Mahidpur.
Baji Rao II was pensioned off to Bithur near Kanpur; the Peshwaship was abolished (1818).
The Treaty of Gwalior (1817) with Scindia and the Treaty of Mandasor (1818) with Holkar closed the war.
Ranjit Singh signed the Treaty of Amritsar (1809) with Metcalfe, fixing the Sutlej as boundary.
First Anglo-Sikh War (1845–46) battles: Mudki, Ferozeshah, Aliwal and Sobraon.
The Treaty of Lahore (9 March 1846) ended the First War; Kashmir went to Gulab Singh (Treaty of Amritsar 1846).
The Treaty of Bhairowal (1846) put a British Resident (Henry Lawrence) in charge at Lahore.
The Second War (1848–49) began with the revolt of Diwan Mulraj at Multan.
Second War battles: Ramnagar, Chillianwala and Gujrat (decisive, 21 Feb 1849).
Dalhousie annexed Punjab on 29 March 1849; Duleep Singh was pensioned.
